questions.q: The CAP theorem says that during a network partition a system must choose between which two properties?
o: Consistency and availability
Consistency and partition tolerance
Availability and low latency
Durability and throughput
questions.w: Partitions happen, so partition tolerance is not optional. The real choice during one is consistency (refuse some requests) or availability (answer, possibly stale).

questions.q: A bank's ledger node cannot reach the other replicas. It rejects writes until the partition heals. Which choice is this?
o: CP: it chooses consistency over availability
AP: it chooses availability over consistency
Neither, since this is simply a bug
Eventual consistency between replicas
questions.w: Rejecting requests to avoid divergent data is the CP trade-off. AP systems keep serving and reconcile later.

questions.q: A client calls a payment service and the request times out. What can the client conclude?
o: Nothing for sure, the payment may or may not have happened
The payment definitely failed, so retry freely
The payment definitely succeeded, so do nothing
The network is down and the client can stop
questions.w: This is why retries need idempotency keys. Without one, a retry can charge twice.

questions.q: What does an idempotent operation guarantee?
o: Repeating it has the same effect as doing it once
It is guaranteed to succeed on the first try
It always runs in constant time
It is never retried by clients
questions.w: `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent by definition. `POST` is not, so add an idempotency key for payments.

questions.q: Why can't you rely on wall-clock timestamps from different servers to order events?
o: Clocks drift and are never perfectly synchronised
Timestamps are too large to store in a database
Servers always run in different time zones
Only databases are allowed to keep a clock
questions.w: Use logical clocks, version vectors or a single sequencer when order matters. Even NTP leaves skew of milliseconds or more.

questions.q: Quorum reads and writes (R + W > N) are used to:
o: Any read overlaps at least one replica with the latest write
Writes become faster than reads on every node
Replication is no longer needed for durability
A leader is elected without any voting
questions.w: With N=3, W=2 and R=2 the read and write sets always share a node, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write.

questions.q: What problem does consensus (Raft, Paxos) solve?
o: Getting several nodes to agree on a value despite failures
Compressing the traffic between data centres
Encrypting messages before they are sent
Balancing HTTP requests across web servers
questions.w: Coordination services like etcd and ZooKeeper use consensus for leader election, configuration and locks.

questions.q: A leader is elected and then loses connectivity, while a new leader takes over. What mechanism stops the old leader from corrupting data?
o: Fencing tokens or epochs that storage rejects when stale
Hoping the old leader notices the change soon
Using longer timeouts on every client
Restarting every client in the cluster
questions.w: Each election increments a number. Storage refuses writes carrying an older number, so a zombie leader cannot win.
